newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Africans urge governments to bolster bourse growth.
newsitem.headline: Africans urge governments to bolster bourse growth.

text.p: African bourse executives said on Friday their markets were still mostly small and inefficient and urged governments to help bolster growth by streamlining banking and protecting foreign investors.
They said they recognised African bourses suffered from low liquidity blamed on barriers to foreign investment, weak banking systems and weak enforcement of regulations governing stock exchanges.

The African bourse executives and regulators spoke in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa on the sidelines of a conference of finance ministers and Western lenders called by the U.N. Economic Commission for Africa. They left for home on Friday.
The bourse executives urged African governments to enhance economic and stuctural reforms that yield macroeconomic results and attract the attention of international investors.
"African capital markets are at a rudimentary stage," George Akamiokhor, director-general of the Securities and Exchange Commission of Nigeria, said in a statement.
"In January 1997, they represented 10 percent of emerging markets' listings, less than 15 percent of emerging markets' capitalisation and two percent of trading value," he added.

Akamiokhor urged governments to foster political stability including pluralist politics and observance of laws, financial sector reforms to keep inflation down and free interest rates and to sell public companies in order to help bourses grow.

Lemma Senbet, professor of finance at the University of Maryland, said enthusiam in stock markets in Africa was marked by a surge in Wall Street interest in Africa, with an increase in investment funds being traded in New York and Europe to $1 billion from zero only five years ago.

Statistics issued by the bourse executives showed however shares on African markets were rarely traded. Turnover ranged from 0.1 percent in Swaziland to a maximum of 10 percent in Botswana. Nigeria had 0.8 percent, Kenya 2.8 percent, Ivory Coast 2.2 percent, Namibia 1.6 percent and Ghana 1.6 percent.
The statistics excluded the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the biggest on the world's poorest continent.
Akamiokhor, who chaired the consultations on African markets, urged governments to launch policies to stimulate the growth of pension funds, insurance companies and unit trusts.
The African Capital Markets Forum (ACMF) said growth of capital markets was in line with economic reforms in Africa.
Senbet saw some of impediments to African capital markets' growth as poor brokerage services and slow settlements, poor accounting and disclosure standards and distortionary taxes.

"There are other drawbacks such as lack of liquidity, low levels of professionalism, inefficient facilities, few financial instruments and intermediaries, low levels of market awareness, inadequate and poor flow of information and a weak regulatory framework," ACMF said in a statement sent to Reuters.
The U.N. Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) said most companies in Africa were owned by individuals or families which were apprehensive about losing control if they floated shares.
"Development of capital markets in Africa will invariably require a shift in both ownership and control of some of these firms to the public through equity holdings," ECA said.
But the bourse executives also said recent mainly economic reforms in Africa had helped the growth of stock exchanges such as those in Ghana, Ivory Coast, Egypt, Morocco and Zimbabwe.
